transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-21
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Elena (Head Cloud Arch), Samir (Security), Priya (Network), Tom (Platform Ops)

Summary section (auto):
- Quick qual: timeframe ~Q3 pilot, production H2 2027 depending on security review.
- Focus: Private deployment inside customer VPCs, require fixed egress IPs and region gating (no PII outside EU/NA).
- Actions: send templates, schedule technical deep dive.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intro — I'm Maya on AE, Jonah's our SE; we'll kick off with a couple discovery questions then dive into network constraints. Elena, do you want to start with objectives for the call?
[00:18] Elena (Customer): Sure, thanks. Um, high level — we're evaluating Redwood for inference for a couple of internal products. Primary requirement is that the inference plane be in our VPC, control egress, and ensure data never leaves specific regions. We're focused on private deployment, not hosted.
[00:32] Jonah (Redwood): Got it. When you say "control egress" do you mean static egress IPs for outbound calls, or just that no data leaves the region?
[00:41] Samir (Customer): Both, actually. We need predictable egress for allowlisting with downstream partners and we have regulatory constraints around EU data residency for certain datasets.
[00:52] Maya (Redwood): Makes sense. Quick qual questions — timeline for pilot? Who owns networking on your side?
[00:59] Elena (Customer): Pilot target is late July, production hopefully Q4. Priya and Tom are our networking/platform owners, Samir is security review lead.
[01:08] Priya (Customer): We run most infra in us-west-2 and eu-west-1; we also have a locked-down ap-southeast-1 presence but that's not in scope for pilot.
[01:18] Jonah (Redwood): Excellent — that helps. For Private we support two main onramp patterns: VPC peering to a Redwood-private VPC for endpoints, or private endpoints via cross-account privatelink style setup. Both have tradeoffs.
[01:31] Tom (Customer): Can you, uh, clarify the peering model? We use a central transit gateway and multiple inbox VPCs. Is Redwood expecting peer to each spoke?
[01:41] Jonah (Redwood): Good question. Options: 1) Peer each spoke to a Redwood consumption VPC — simple but scale concern if you have hundreds of spokes. 2) Bring up a Redwood-managed TGW attachment in your account and route via transit — that's the recommended for multi-VPC shops. 3) PrivateLink/endpoint: we can publish interface endpoints in your account but that requires endpoint services and cross-account setup.
[02:05] Priya (Customer): We prefer using our transit gateway path, but I want to understand NAT and egress IPs — if the inference runs in our VPC, does Redwood still require outbound to S3 or third-party services?
[02:18] Jonah (Redwood): For Private, data plane stays in your VPC. Storage access (model artifacts, logs) can be configured to pull from your S3 via VPC endpoints. For telemetry and control-plane calls we can route over the private control plane or use customer endpoints. We do have optional egress dependencies for license checks if you opt into hosted model catalog, but you can bring-your-own-model (BYOM) to avoid that.
[02:40] Samir (Customer): License check — is that over the public internet? We can't allow that.
[02:45] Maya (Redwood): We can do license/telemetry over a private peering or via a secure mTLS channel to our control plane in your account — we have a private control plane option. We'll include details in the checklist.
[02:57] Elena (Customer): Ok. Another thing — we need a fixed egress IP for outbound calls so downstream partners can allowlist. How does Redwood handle that?
[03:05] Jonah (Redwood): Two approaches: run NAT in your VPC (you control the egress IPs) — simplest. Or we can front proxy egress through a Redwood-managed NAT with static egress IPs per customer but that requires a managed contract and more network setup. For regulatory reasons most customers prefer customer-owned NAT.
[03:24] Tom (Customer): If we do customer NAT, do you require changes to route tables on our side?
[03:29] Jonah (Redwood): Minimal. You'll need routes for traffic to the model-serving subnets and potentially a dedicated route table for Redwood subnets. We'll share terraform snippets.
[03:39] Priya (Customer): Okay. About private endpoints — we have a policy that only approved endpoint services can be created. Cross-account endpoints are regulated; can Redwood run the endpoint service in our account?
[03:51] Maya (Redwood): Yes, we can initiate a cross-account endpoint service where Redwood registers an endpoint service and you create interface endpoints in your account. Alternatively, we can run the compute in your VPC (bring the images) which avoids cross-account endpoints entirely.
[04:05] Samir (Customer): Running compute in our VPC — that sounds like on-prem style. Is that your Private offering? How much operational overhead on our side?
[04:13] Jonah (Redwood): It's our Private mode — we ship a control plane that lives in Redwood but compute can be run in a customer VPC (we call it customer-hosted runtime). Operationally we automate node lifecycle, but your team would own VPC subnets, security groups, and upgrades can be coordinated with our ops team.
[04:29] Elena (Customer): And for crypto — we require KMS integration and HSM-backed key storage for model keys and logs.
[04:36] Maya (Redwood): We support KMS integrations (AWS KMS, CloudHSM) for both data-at-rest and in-flight key wrapping; we'll include KMS configuration examples.
[04:45] Tom (Customer): Audit logs — how long do you store them, and can we ship to our own S3/CloudWatch?
[04:51] Jonah (Redwood): You can ship audit logs to your own S3/CloudWatch; retention is configurable. For Private deployments customers usually keep logs in their own account for compliance.
[04:59] Samir (Customer): We need SOC2 and ISO artifacts before a security sign-off. Do you have those as downloadable PDFs?
[05:06] Maya (Redwood): Yes — we'll attach SOC2 Type II summary and a security pack. Expect those in the checklist.
[05:12] Elena (Customer): Great. On region gating — we want inference for EU data to stay strictly in eu-west-1. Is that configurable per model or per route?
[05:22] Jonah (Redwood): We do routing policies that can be per-route or per-tenant. For example you can pin model deployments to specific AZ/region and the runtime will enforce region-only scheduling. We'll share docs on model pinning and region isolation. Note: some open model caches might be hosted in other regions unless BYOM is used.
[05:45] Priya (Customer): Ah — cache locations. We can't have cached KV data in non-EU regions. How is KV cache placement handled?
[05:52] Jonah (Redwood): KV cache follows the serving instance; with Private and BYOM cache stays in your VPC. If you use Redwood-hosted caches across regions, that's a different config and not acceptable for your constraint.
[06:05] Tom (Customer): For initial pilot, we just want a single region deployment in us-west-2 for internal tools, and a separate EU pilot later. So two isolated pilots.
[06:14] Maya (Redwood): That works. We'll recommend starting with us-west-2 where latency is best for your users, then replicate.
[06:20] Elena (Customer): Bandwidth concerns — inference API traffic could be heavy. Do you recommend dedicated subnets and autoscaling?
[06:28] Jonah (Redwood): Yes — dedicate subnets and security groups. Autoscaling is supported; sizing depends on expected qps and token lengths. Our Optimize team can estimate cost/throughput after you provide sample workloads. We'll ask for token distribution in the checklist.
[06:44] Samir (Customer): Back to egress: what about third-party telemetry, e.g., Sentry or NewRelic — can those be sent to our endpoints?
[06:52] Jonah (Redwood): You can configure telemetry to your endpoints — most customers ship telemetry to their own observability stack. We'll include configuration for that.
[07:00] Maya (Redwood): Quick note — Elastic IPs for static egress can be attached to NAT gateways in your account. If you want Redwood-managed static egress we have a detailed security review for that.
[07:12] Priya (Customer): If we go via transit gateway, do we need to update route propagation to avoid hairpinning?
[07:18] Jonah (Redwood): We'll work with your network team on route tables. Typical pattern: create a dedicated route table for Redwood subnets and propagate only routes needed for model traffic. We'll show recommended CIDR ranges to avoid overlap.
[07:33] Tom (Customer): CIDR overlap is a pain — we already have addresses in 10.0.0.0/8. Do you have recommended ranges?
[07:40] Jonah (Redwood): We'll provide a non-overlapping suggestion (e.g., 172.20.240.0/22) and terraform snippets to reserve them in your tenancy.
[07:52] Elena (Customer): What about IP allowlisting for the control plane? Our security wants a list of IPs to open.
[07:58] Maya (Redwood): For private control plane we don't require public IPs; if you want public egress for control-plane calls we'll provide IP ranges, but most customers go private. We'll add both options to the checklist.
[08:12] Samir (Customer): Any customer references with similar constraints?
[08:17] Maya (Redwood): Yes — we recently onboarded a fintech with transit-gateway flow and KMS in eu-west-1. We'll share a short case study link.
[08:24] Elena (Customer): Perfect. Can you talk high level about failover — if a region goes down, do you fail to hosted or degrade?
[08:32] Jonah (Redwood): For Private deployments we support failover policies: you can set strict region-only, or allow fallback to a cold-standby in another region (with either a model warmup or degraded throughput). For strict compliance where data must not leave the region, you pick region-only and app handles degraded service.
[08:50] Priya (Customer): Regarding upgrades — how do you handle rolling upgrades without KV cache eviction?
[08:56] Jonah (Redwood): We use draining and continuous KV migration to avoid eviction. There are small windows for model reload, but we preserve cache between instance handoffs when possible. We'll include our runbook.
[09:10] Tom (Customer): Are there any limitations around GPUs or instance types in our VPC?
[09:15] Jonah (Redwood): We'll need EC2/GPU quotas in your account for customer-hosted runtimes. We can provide instance family recommendations (A100/RTX or Graviton+Inferentia depending) and fallback to CPU for lightweight workloads.
[09:29] Elena (Customer): Cost question — is Dedicated cheaper per-token than Private?
[09:34] Maya (Redwood): Often Dedicated (Redwood-managed reserved capacity) can be more cost-effective at scale because of pooling, but Private gives you isolation and can be cheaper if you already own GPU fleet or get lower instance costs in your contracts. We'll prepare an apples-to-apples estimate.
[09:49] Samir (Customer): Security controls we care about: SSO/SAML, RBAC, audited changes to model deployments, and KMS. How are those surfaced?
[09:58] Jonah (Redwood): SSO/SAML and RBAC available in Console; for Private we can integrate with your IdP. Deployment audit logs are forwardable to your SIEM.
[10:07] Priya (Customer): Any network sniffing or packet capture restrictions? We have rules about inspecting traffic — we can't allow third-party packet capture in our VPC.
[10:15] Jonah (Redwood): We don't require packet capture. Debug traces are application-level and can be forwarded to your observability stack.
[10:23] Maya (Redwood): Quick pause — I'm going to share the checklist link in chat, it's a living doc. Link: https://app.redwood.ai/docs/private-checklist (note: placeholder).
[10:31] Elena (Customer): Got it. We'll review.
[10:35] Tom (Customer): One more operational — who owns upgrades and security patches for runtime containers?
[10:41] Jonah (Redwood): For customer-hosted runtime, Redwood coordinates upgrades but you can opt-in for maintenance windows. We sign security patches; they can be pushed automatically or gated for your approval.
[10:52] Samir (Customer): Our procurement will ask about indemnity and data processing agreements.
[10:57] Maya (Redwood): We'll route legal through our channel and attach our standard DPA and security addendum to the checklist.
[11:03] Elena (Customer): If we wanted a small pilot, what's minimum footprint?
[11:07] Jonah (Redwood): A typical pilot is 2-3 GPU nodes in a single subnet, with autoscaling policies. We can run a proof-of-performance for your payload — we just need sample prompts and token distribution.
[11:18] Priya (Customer): We'll send sample traffic next week.
[11:21] Maya (Redwood): Great. Any blockers we haven't covered?
[11:25] Elena (Customer): Not yet, I think we got the main concerns.
[11:28] Tom (Customer): One micro thing — do you support IPv6-only VPCs?
[11:32] Jonah (Redwood): Currently we need IPv4 for control-plane compatibility; we can discuss IPv6 plans but recommend IPv4 for now.
[11:41] Priya (Customer): Noted.
[11:44] Maya (Redwood): Ok recap — action items and next steps: we'll send the checklist, security pack, terraform snippets, and SOC2 artifacts; set up the deep-dive with Jonah and your SRE for late next week.
[11:58] Elena (Customer): Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[12:01] Maya (Redwood): Thank you — we'll follow up by email with the artifacts and proposed calendar invites.
[12:08] End of call.

References/links mentioned during the call:
- Private checklist (shared): https://app.redwood.ai/docs/private-checklist
- Terraform snippet repo (to be sent): https://github.com/redwood-inference/private-terraform-examples
- SOC2 and security pack (to attach): /redwood/security/soc2-summary.pdf

Notes on transcript quality: speaker turns are reasonably accurate though some proper nouns may be slightly mistranscribed (e.g., endpoint service names). Occasional filler words and overlaps present.
